newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: New law seen unlikely to improve Slovak sell-offs.
newsitem.headline: New law seen unlikely to improve Slovak sell-offs.

text.p: The Slovak parliament returned the right of direct privatisation to the government on Friday, raising analyst fears that little would change in the country's murky privatisation process.

Parliament approved an amendment to the privatisation law handing the government responsibility for direct sales of state assets, once the domain of the state privatisation agency, the National Property Fund (NPF).
The new law brings privatisation procedures in line with a Constitutional Court ruling made last November which said the government, and not the NPF, was responsible for direct privatisation.
"This will not change much...the NFP was controlled by people close to the ruling coalition anyway," said Ivan Miklos, an economic analyst at independent think-tank Mesa 10.

"The only difference is that you will be able to directly point at the government and accuse it of bad privatisation. But we should not expect the cabinet will suddenly change the method of selling the state assets to a more transparent way just because of this law," he added.
The new version of the law is not retroactive, and the government has said that it would not overturn any previous sales agreed to by the NPF.

Privatisation has long been one of the hottest political issues in Slovakia, with the opposition repeatedly alleging cronyism, a claim the government denies saying it has had no influence on NPF which is an independent legal entity.
Neither opposition parties in parliament, nor the Highest Control Office have been able to supervise the country's privatisation process.
Over the past three years, Slovakia has scrapped mass voucher privatisation and directly sold off stakes in a number of leading companies without public tenders.
Few details of the sales are ever revealed and the names of the buyers, often linked to company management, rarely mean anything -- even to Slovak market watchers.
Foreign institutions, including the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), have also criticised the Slovak privatisation process for lack of transparency.

For example, the EBRD took a 10.5 percent stake in oil refinery Slovnaft in 1995 when it bought half the refiner's $113 million issue of global depositary receipts which flopped on international markets.
The London-based development bank, set up to encourage free market reforms in post-communist Europe, effectively paid the 1,000 crowns ($32.09) per share face value.
But shortly afterwards, the NPF sold another 39 percent of Slovnaft to a management-led consortium called Slovintegra at an implied prices of just 156 crowns per share.
Analysts noted the new law will not affect state assets turned to stakes in joint-stock companies and managed by the NPF.

"The new law will only affect the currently state-owned firms, and those state-controlled joint-stock companies will remain fully under NPF control," said one analysts who did not wish to be named. "It will not, for example, affect state stakes in largest commercial banks held by the NPF," he added.
